context.description: Burra grew around the Monster Mine, a copper mine worked from the 1840s, and it is one of the Australian sites in a World Heritage bid for Cornish copper mining. The mine site, the Redruth Gaol and the creek-bank dugouts where early miners lived all lie within a few kilometres of Market Square. The Burra Heritage Passport, running since 1979, lends a key to 11 locked National Heritage sites. Museums and a restored railway station fill out the town.

context.description: Port Lincoln sits on Boston Bay at the southern tip of the Eyre Peninsula and is known as Australia's seafood capital. Tuna and other seafood come off the working harbour, and boats leave from here for great white shark cage diving. Lookouts, a murals trail and a maritime museum fill a day in town, and Lincoln National Park and Whalers Way lie a short drive south.

context.description: Lincoln National Park overlooks Boston Bay on the southern Eyre Peninsula, with granite headlands, sheltered bays and offshore islands. On its southern side the Sleaford-Wanna dunes meet the surf of the Southern Ocean. Visitors walk cliff-top and beach trails, camp by the water and watch for whales in winter, and the secluded Memory Cove is reached by booking a gate key.

context.description: Coffin Bay is a small village on the western side of the Eyre Peninsula, about 40 minutes' drive from Port Lincoln. Matthew Flinders named the bay after his friend Sir Isaac Coffin, and the town is known for its oysters. Coffin Bay National Park to the west has windswept cliffs, dunes, surf beaches and sheltered bays, and Kellidie Bay Conservation Park lies to the east. An 8 km foreshore trail follows the shore past the jetty and the oyster-growing waters.
